bond-enthalpies-s1.title: Average bond enthalpies
bond-enthalpies-s1.text: Average bond enthalpies for bonds in gas-phase molecules. Use them for every item in this set.

bond-enthalpies-s2.title: Two steps of a reaction on paper
bond-enthalpies-s2.html:
A student models H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g) in two imaginary steps.

Step 1. H–H + Cl–Cl → 2 H + 2 Cl (all bonds broken; separate atoms)

Step 2. 2 H + 2 Cl → 2 H–Cl (new bonds formed)

Bond enthalpies: H–H 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl 242 kJ/mol, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol.

items.q: Estimate ΔH, in kJ/mol, for CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(g). (CO₂ is O=C=O; water is H–O–H.)

mistakes.why: Value: you counted one of each bond. Count every bond: 4 C–H and 2 O=O break; 2 C=O and 4 O–H form.
Value: two O₂ molecules react, so two O=O bonds break (2 × 495 kJ).

items.q: Estimate ΔH, in kJ/mol, for the hydrogenation of ethene: H₂C=CH₂(g) + H–H(g) → H₃C–CH₃(g).

mistakes.why: Value: ethane has six C–H bonds and ethene four, so two new C–H bonds form, not one.
Value: you left out the H–H bond that breaks and the two C–H bonds that form.

why.correct: Only the changed bonds matter (the four C–H bonds of ethene stay). Broken: C=C + H–H = 614 + 436 = 1050 kJ. Formed: C–C + 2 C–H = 348 + 2(413) = 1174 kJ. ΔH ≈ 1050 − 1174 = −124 kJ/mol.

items.q: Estimate ΔH, in kJ/mol, for N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g).

mistakes.why: Value: two NH₃ molecules form, each with three N–H bonds: six N–H bonds in all.
Value: three H₂ molecules react, so three H–H bonds break.

items.q: The measured ΔH for N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g) is −92.2 kJ/mol. Why does the estimate from the table differ slightly?
options: The estimate counts the bonds broken but leaves out the bonds formed.
Bond enthalpies give the energy released when bonds break, so the sign is reversed.
The measured value includes energy to melt the ammonia, which the estimate leaves out.
The table lists averages over many molecules, not the N–H bond strength in NH₃ itself.

why.correct: Bond enthalpies are averages for a bond type across many compounds, so a bond-enthalpy ΔH is an estimate; here −97 kJ/mol versus −92.2 kJ/mol measured.
options: Both are counted: ΔH ≈ broken − formed.
Breaking a bond absorbs energy, and the sign of the estimate matches the measured value.
All three substances are gases at these conditions; nothing melts.
Right: an N–H bond's strength depends on the rest of the molecule; 391 kJ/mol is an average.

items.q: Using the table, which reaction is predicted to release the most energy per mole of reaction?
options: H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2 HF(g)
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g)
CH₄(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₃Cl(g) + HCl(g)
N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g)

why.correct: Most exothermic: weak bonds broken, strong bonds formed. F–F (155) is weak and H–F (567) is very strong, giving −543 kJ/mol.
options: Right: 436 + 155 − 2(567) = −543 kJ/mol: weak F–F broken, very strong H–F formed.
436 + 242 − 2(431) = −184 kJ/mol, much less than for HF.
2249 − 2346 = −97 kJ/mol: the very strong N≡N bond costs a lot to break.

items.q: What is the enthalpy change for Step 1?
options: −678 kJ, because breaking bonds releases energy
+678 kJ, because breaking bonds absorbs energy
+862 kJ, because two bonds are broken
0 kJ, because no new substance is made

why.correct: Step 1 breaks H–H (436 kJ) and Cl–Cl (242 kJ): ΔH₁ = +678 kJ, endothermic.
options: Bonded atoms attract each other; separating them takes energy, so the sign is positive.
Right: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ must be supplied to pull the atoms apart.
The two bonds broken are H–H and Cl–Cl, not two H–Cl bonds.
Separating atoms changes the energy even though no product has formed yet.

items.q: What is the enthalpy change for Step 2?
options: +862 kJ, because forming bonds requires energy
−431 kJ, because one H–Cl bond forms
−862 kJ, because forming two H–Cl bonds releases energy
−184 kJ, because that is the overall change

why.correct: Forming bonds releases energy: ΔH₂ = −2 × 431 = −862 kJ.
options: Atoms that attract each other release energy as they bond.
Two HCl molecules form, so two H–Cl bonds: 2 × 431.
Right: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ is released as the atoms bond.
−184 kJ is the overall ΔH, the sum of Steps 1 and 2, not Step 2 alone.

items.q: Add the two steps to estimate ΔH, in kJ/mol, for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g).

mistakes.why: Value: two H–Cl bonds form. Use 2 × 431 kJ for the bonds formed.
Value: forming bonds releases energy, so Step 2 is −862 kJ. Subtract the bonds formed.

why.correct: ΔH ≈ ΔH₁ + ΔH₂ = +678 kJ + (−862 kJ) = −184 kJ/mol. The same result as "bonds broken − bonds formed".

items.q: Which statement explains, at the particle level, why the overall reaction is exothermic?
options: The H–Cl bonds formed are stronger in total than the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds broken.
Breaking the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds releases more energy than forming H–Cl absorbs.
Each H–Cl bond is stronger than each H–H bond, so less energy is needed overall.
The reaction makes more molecules than it uses, which releases energy.

why.correct: Total bonds formed (2 × 431 = 862 kJ) outweigh total bonds broken (436 + 242 = 678 kJ), so 184 kJ is released per mole of reaction.
options: Right: forming 862 kJ worth of bonds releases more than the 678 kJ needed to break the old ones.
This reverses both signs: breaking absorbs and forming releases.
An H–Cl bond (431) is actually weaker than an H–H bond (436); the totals decide.
Two molecules react and two form; molecule count is not the reason.

items.q: Which expression gives ΔH from average bond enthalpies?
options: Sum of bond enthalpies of bonds formed − sum of bond enthalpies of bonds broken
Sum of bond enthalpies of bonds broken − sum of bond enthalpies of bonds formed
Sum of bond enthalpies of the products − sum of bond enthalpies of the reactants
Sum of bond enthalpies of the bonds in the reactants and products

why.correct: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Breaking bonds costs energy (+); forming them pays energy back (−).
options: This gives the right size with the wrong sign. Bonds broken come first.
Right: energy in to break bonds, minus energy out from forming them.
This is the "products minus reactants" habit; with bond enthalpies it gives the wrong sign.
Breaking and forming have opposite signs, so they cannot simply be added.

items.q: Bond enthalpies are always given as positive numbers. What does that mean?
options: Forming any bond requires energy to be added.
A reaction that breaks bonds is endothermic overall.
Breaking any bond requires energy to be added.
Bonds store energy that is released when they break.

why.correct: A bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break 1 mol of a bond in gas-phase molecules, so it is positive. Forming that bond releases the same amount.
options: Forming a bond releases energy; the positive number is for breaking.
Most reactions break and form bonds; the overall sign depends on the balance.
Right: a bond enthalpy is the energy absorbed to break 1 mol of bonds in the gas phase.
This common idea is backward: energy is released when bonds form.

items.q: For H₂(g) + Br₂(g) → 2 HBr(g), ΔH = −103 kJ/mol. The H–H bond enthalpy is 436 kJ/mol and the Br–Br bond enthalpy is 193 kJ/mol. Estimate the H–Br bond enthalpy, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: check the sign of ΔH. −103 = 629 − 2x gives 2x = 732, not 526.
Value: two H–Br bonds form, so divide the total for bonds formed by 2.

why.correct: ΔH = broken − formed: −103 = (436 + 193) − 2x. So 2x = 629 + 103 = 732, and x = 366 kJ/mol.

items.q: Two reactions break bonds with the same total bond enthalpy. Reaction 1 forms bonds with a total of 900 kJ; Reaction 2 forms bonds with a total of 700 kJ. Which is true?
options: Reaction 1 releases 200 kJ more energy than Reaction 2.
Reaction 2 releases 200 kJ more energy than Reaction 1.
Both release the same energy, since they break the same bonds.
Reaction 1 absorbs 200 kJ more energy than Reaction 2.

why.correct: With the same bonds broken, ΔH(1) − ΔH(2) = −900 − (−700) = −200 kJ: Reaction 1 releases 200 kJ more.
options: Right: ΔH = broken − formed, so a larger "formed" total makes ΔH 200 kJ more negative.
Forming stronger bonds releases more energy, which favors Reaction 1.
The bonds formed differ, so the energy released differs.
More energy released by bond formation makes ΔH more negative, not more positive.

items.q: A student says, "Fuels like gasoline store energy in their bonds, and the energy is released when those bonds break." Which statement best corrects this?
options: Breaking the fuel's bonds releases energy, but just at a high temperature.
Breaking the fuel's bonds absorbs energy; burning releases energy because the bonds formed in CO₂ and H₂O are stronger.
The energy comes from the oxygen's bonds breaking, not the fuel's.
The energy comes from the fuel's bonds getting stronger as it burns.

why.correct: Energy is released when bonds form. Burning a fuel is exothermic because the C=O and O–H bonds formed in CO₂ and H₂O release more energy than breaking the fuel's bonds and the O=O bonds absorbs; for methane, 2 C=O and 4 O–H formed outweigh 4 C–H and 2 O=O broken.
options: Breaking bonds absorbs energy at any temperature.
Right: the energy comes from the difference, with strong product bonds forming.
Breaking O=O bonds also absorbs energy.
The fuel molecules are taken apart; new, stronger bonds form in the products.

items.q: Using H–H 436, O=O 495 and O–H 463 kJ/mol, what is the estimated ΔH for 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(g)?
options: +485 kJ/mol
+5 kJ/mol
−485 kJ/mol
+441 kJ/mol

why.correct: Count every bond: 2 H–H and 1 O=O broken; 2 × 2 = 4 O–H formed. ΔH ≈ 1367 − 1852 = −485 kJ/mol.
options: Size right, sign wrong: you subtracted broken from formed.
You counted one H–H bond and two O–H bonds; two H₂ react and two H₂O (four O–H) form.
Each water molecule has two O–H bonds, so four O–H bonds form.

items.q: Which statements about bond enthalpies are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A double bond between two atoms has a larger bond enthalpy than a single bond between the same atoms.
A bond-enthalpy ΔH is usually an estimate, because table values are averages.
Bond enthalpies give accurate ΔH values for reactions involving liquids and solids.
A reaction that breaks strong bonds and forms weak ones is exothermic.
Breaking 1 mol of C–H bonds releases 413 kJ.

why.correct: Bond enthalpies are positive averages for gas-phase bonds; breaking absorbs, forming releases, and multiple bonds are stronger.
options: More shared electron pairs hold the atoms more strongly: C=C (614) > C–C (348).
The same bond type has slightly different strengths in different molecules.
They are for gas-phase molecules; attractions between molecules in liquids and solids are not included.
Strong bonds broken and weak bonds formed means more energy absorbed than released, so the reaction is endothermic.
Breaking bonds absorbs energy: 413 kJ is absorbed.
